extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students and activists interested in sociology of race, crime and policing (especially Britain)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical sociological analysis of 'mugging' as a social and political phenomenon that links race, class, crime and policing; intended to inform theory, strategy and political practice. Focuses on evaluating causes, meanings and the adequacy of responses and organising strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Race as central structural modality
rubrics_metrics.description: Race is intrinsic to the manner in which the black labouring classes are constituted at economic, political and ideological levels: 'Race is the modality in which class is lived. It is also the medium in which class relations are experienced.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses and strategies must treat race as constitutive (not merely a colouring) of class relations. When measuring adequacy of struggle, assess whether it addresses the racially-structured reproduction of black labour across economic, political and ideological levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime as a predictable product of capitalist structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime is a comprehensible consequence of the processes that subordinate black labour ('Crime is one perfectly predictable and quite comprehensible consequence of this process').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations should link criminal behaviour to structural economic processes (exploitation, marginalisation, formation of reserve armies of labour) rather than treating it as solely moral failing or individual pathology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish criminal adaptation from political act
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime, though sometimes arising from social/economic exploitation, 'contains no solution' and 'is not a political act' as such; only in certain circumstances can it express oppositional class consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether criminal acts have political content, examine context (who the victims are, class position, whether actions 'give a muffled and displaced expression' to permanent exclusion) rather than assuming crime equals politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful evaluation of 'wagelessness' interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two ways to understand wagelessness: (a) as evidence of a quasi-political refusal to work expressing new mass-worker consciousness; (b) as economic necessity where 'refusal' is largely a virtue of necessity with many who would take work if offered it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims that refusal-to-work is political by empirically distinguishing voluntary, politicised refusal from forced unemployment; avoid overstating the political content of survival-driven criminality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not uncritically label marginalised black labour as lumpenproletariat
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a marginalised sector may depend on crime for survival, it is not automatically a classical lumpenproletariat in position, consciousness or role relative to capital; colonial and metropolitan histories complicate the label.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify social strata by examining their structural relation to capital (position in production/reserve army), consciousness and historical formation; avoid glossing over mechanisms by using convenience labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative autonomy of economic, political and ideological levels
rubrics_metrics.description: The levels of the social formation (economic, political, ideological) have relative autonomy and require independent 'means of representation'—there is not necessarily a straightforward correspondence between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses and strategies must account for discontinuities between levels; success or transformation at one level (e.g., economic) does not automatically translate into political or ideological gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure adequacy of struggle against the structures it aims to transform
rubrics_metrics.description: Race provides 'one of the criteria by which we measure the adequacy of struggle to the structures it aims to transform.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political struggles by whether they engage the racially-conditioned mechanisms through which black labour is reproduced (do tactics/organising correspond to structural dynamics at all relevant levels?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware mistaking proto-political consciousness for organised politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of criminal or 'resistance-consciousness' may appear as proto-political but are not the same as organised political consciousness or struggle: 'It constitutes a power, but it is a mistake to mistake a proto-political consciousness for organised political consciousness and practice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume spontaneous street-level adaptations will evolve into sustained political organisation; strategic intervention and organisation are required to translate consciousness into political force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organising and alliances must acknowledge structurally produced divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal divisions of the working class articulate themselves along racial lines because they are produced by structure; tactics for unity must recognise real material bases rather than assume simple fraternal solidarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing united fronts or tactical alliances, analyse material interests and sectional needs; solidarity may be necessary but must be built on an understanding of how race structures class relations and reproduces divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend criminalised fractions to avoid permanent marginalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Black organisations and the community often 'defend black youth against harassment'—failure to defend them risks abandoning those driven into crime to permanent criminalisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political practice should include protective strategies for marginalised youth to prevent further criminalisation, while also not romanticising or endorsing criminal acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical approach to moral panics (the 'mugging scare')
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'mugging' scare must be reconstructed and its logic examined rather than reduced to simple moral judgments; media and political responses should be analyzed in terms of underlying structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should trace how incidents are framed in media/policy, how panic structures political responses, and how this framing obscures deeper structural causes and strategic implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical and comparative evidence to assess political potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical examples (colonial struggles, Black Panthers, Battle of Algiers) show that a criminalised stratum can sometimes become a political base, but conditions differ and transferability is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess contemporary political potential by careful historical and comparative analysis; do not assume past successes in different structural contexts imply likely success now.
